# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

```{r}
#| label: disc-numbers
#| include: false

d_inc_win <- p6_res(p6_test_results, "incumbent", "win")
d_mkt_win <- p6_res(p6_test_results, "market-only", "win")
d_inc_ew5 <- p6_res(p6_test_results, "incumbent", "eachway")
gap_win <- -d_inc_win$roi
```

## What this paper found

The betting rule was not the binding constraint either.

Paper 3 concluded that the linear predictor was not what limited the series,
because a tree ensemble tied it. Paper 5 found the feature encoding was worth
something on ranking but nothing on ROI. This paper adds the third: the
selection and staking rule was not it either. Nine selection rules and three
staking rules, searched on five thousand races, produced three declarations,
and all three lost to the rule they were declared to beat.

The uncomfortable part is the control. On the win market a rule that reads no
model output returns `r p6_fmt_pct(d_mkt_win$roi)` against
`r p6_fmt_pct(d_inc_win$roi)` for the model rule, and the paired contrast
between the declared rule and the control contains zero. The model's
contribution to bet selection is not visible on this data. That is consistent
with paper 4, which asked the same question in a different form — what does
the model add *given* the price — and found that against the settled starting
price it adds nothing distinguishable. Two papers, two designs, the same
answer.

## What it did not find

It did not find that the model is worthless. Papers 2b, 3 and 5 measured
ranking, and there the encoder is distinguishably better than every earlier
arm in the series, on nine contrasts with nine intervals excluding zero. A
model can rank better and still not turn that into a bet, because the bet has
to beat a price and the price already contains most of what the ranking
knows.

It did not find that the place result means anything about the model. The
declared place rule beats the market-only control by
`r p6_fmt_pts(p6_con(p6_test_contrasts, "place", "market-only")$diff_point)`
points on an interval excluding zero, and that is the only such interval in
the paper. It is a statement about a synthetic place market that prices
favourites hardest, not about model skill: the same rule is
indistinguishable from the incumbent it was declared to beat.

## Limitations {#sec-limitations}

**The rules were searched on in-sample predictions.** The model was fitted on
the training races, so its probabilities there are sharper than anything it
produces out of sample, and every training ROI that reads a model probability
is inflated (@sec-insample). The ranking the declaration rule read is
therefore a ranking under contamination, and it plausibly favoured the arms
that lean hardest on the model's in-sample sharpness — which is exactly the
class of rule that then bet almost nothing on test. A search set built from
out-of-fold predictions, or from a nested split inside the training half,
would be a better search set and is the first change to make if this is taken
further.

**The model was selected with knowledge of these test races.** The betting
rule was not — it was declared and committed before any test target existed —
but five papers of model development have looked at this test split, and the
encoder that scores it here is the one those five papers arrived at. The
model side of every number in this paper carries that history. Only the
betting-rule side is clean.

**The intervals are wide.** The declared win rule stakes
`r sprintf("%.0f", p6_res(p6_test_results, "^declared", "win")$total_stake)`
units across `r p6_comma(n_test_races)` races and its interval is
`r p6_fmt_pct_ci(p6_res(p6_test_results, "^declared", "win")$ci_lo, p6_res(p6_test_results, "^declared", "win")$ci_hi)`.
No conclusion rests on it, and none should. The comparisons that carry weight
are the ones on full-universe arms: S1/K0 and S4/K0, both betting a thousand
races or more.

**Two thousand test races is not many for a betting question.** A rule with a
true edge of two points would need far more races than this to separate from
zero at a 90% interval. The right reading of "no interval excludes zero" is
that this design cannot see an edge of the size worth having, not that no
such edge exists.

**Every rule loses money.** That is the result, and it is stated without
qualification: on the test split, at real starting prices, no rule tested in
this paper returns a profit on any of the three markets.

## Break-even, and what would settle it {#sec-breakeven}

The margin decomposition (@sec-margin) puts a number on the gap. The
incumbent loses `r p6_fmt_pct(gap_win)` on the win market at the starting
price and returns `r p6_fmt_pct(d_inc_win$roi_fair)` at a book with the
over-round taken out. Its each-way ROI at paper 5's terms is
`r p6_fmt_pct(d_inc_ew5$roi)`, the closest to break-even in the series. So
the question is not whether the model is a long way from profitable — it is
whether it is roughly one bookmaker's margin away.

The direction that would answer it is prices better than the starting price.
The starting price is the settled price, after the market has absorbed
everything it is going to absorb; paper 4 found the model adds nothing
against it, but adds substantially against the pre-race racecard forecast
published the night before. If a price closer to the forecast than to the
settled price were available at bet time — an exchange price early in the
market, before liquidity builds — the same selection could face a materially
smaller margin, and possibly a positive one.

**This dataset cannot settle that.** Smartform holds the overnight forecast
price and the settled starting price, and nothing in between. There is no
exchange price history: no series of Betfair prices from market open to the
off, no record of what was actually available at any moment, and no depth
alongside it. A rule that looks break-even against a hypothetical fair book
is not evidence that a real counterparty would have taken the bet at that
price, in that size.

What it would take is exchange price and volume history for these races,
timestamped, and a repeat of exactly this design against prices taken at a
declared time before the off rather than at the off. Until that exists, the
honest statement is the one the numbers support: the model does not beat the
settled market, the gap on the best market tested is about the size of the
over-round, and whether an earlier price closes that gap is untested.
